children: Paramount Pictures' Street Fighter vaulted to the top of the domestic box office on Sunday, amid a busy weekend of openings.

The videogame-based action adventure, about estranged street fighters recruited for the World Warrior Tournament only to discover a deadly conspiracy, opened to an estimated $31 million in North American ticket sales.

The movie, one of the first releases from postmerger Skydance, created when Paramount merged with Warner Bros. Discovery earlier this month, topped the international box office with $20.1 million, for a $51.1 million global opening, including $7.7 million on IMAX screens. It stars Andrew Koji, Noah Centineo, and Callina Liang, and is rated PG-13.

But more people seem to be talking about A24's You Can See Everything, the biographical documentary filmed in secret after disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes invited a film crew into her home 34 days before reporting to federal prison for conspiracy and fraud. The nearly three-hour movie grossed $15 million from 855 theaters, an average of $17,544 a theater, according to Rentrak. The R-rated film was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.

A24 reported more than 2,000 sellout screenings, with 70% of moviegoers under age 35, more than 90% of audiences recommending the movie. Rentrak said it ranks as the No. 2 documentary behind Fahrenheit 9/11, which opened with $23.9 million in 2004. It has a 99% Rotten Tomatoes rating among critics and a 98% among audiences.

"Sometimes the biggest story at the box office isn't necessarily the movie that finishes at No. 1," according to Rentrak's head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. Although Street Fighter hauled in a "solid $31 million domestic debut in 3,575 theaters, A24's You Can See Everything is shaping up to be the big story of the weekend."
This weekend's estimated $103.9 million in domestic ticket sales is 48.2% higher than the same weekend last year, when Universal's Black Phone 2 debuted at No. 1 with $27.3 million.

Domestic year-to-date box office through Sunday is an estimated $8.219 billion, 20% higher than at the same point in 2025, according to Rentrak. This year's total is down about 8.5% from this point in 2019, when the box office stood at $8.983 billion.

The range of genres, including action, documentary, horror, survival thriller, and literary adaptation, is "giving very different audiences a reason to go out to the movie theater, an important hallmark of the 2026 marketplace," Dergarabedian said.

Meanwhile, Universal's horror film Other Mommy, about an 8-year-old girl's bond with a sinister entity in her closet, sold an estimated $8.35 million in its second weekend. That brings its domestic total to $44.9 million and its global total to $78.8 million, according to Rentrak.

20th Century Studios' Whalefall, about a scuba diver swallowed by an 80-foot, 60-ton sperm whale, opened in fourth place with an estimated $8 million in domestic box office sales and $17.5 million worldwide. Focus Features' Sense and Sensibility debuted in fifth place with $7.25 million domestically and $18.5 million globally.

Sony and Colombia Pictures' The Social Reckoning, about Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen divulging secrets from the social media company to ex-Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, sold another $1.6 million in its second weekend, bringing its domestic total to $8.3 million and its global total to about $14.3 million.

Filmmaker Alex Gibney's documentary Musk, featuring the SpaceX and Tesla CEO in archival footage, tweets, and a computer-generated simulation, expanded to 472 theaters, selling $306,702 in its second weekend, and bringing its domestic total to $394,912. The nearly-four-hour film, including a 10-minute intermission, has a 97% critics rating on Rotten Tomatoes, but the film's distributor Bleeker Street has said difficulties advertising the film on Musk's X platform and TikTok have hampered awareness about the film.
